content: Carotene refers to a group of related compounds with the chemical formula C40H56. It is an orange pigment that plays a crucial role in photosynthesis by transferring absorbed light energy to chlorophyll. This pigment is responsible for the orange coloration in carrots and various other fruits and vegetables. Chemically, carotene is classified as a terpene, synthesized from eight isoprene units. The primary forms of carotene are alpha-carotene (α-carotene) and beta-carotene (β-carotene), though other forms such as gamma (γ), delta (δ), and epsilon (ε) carotene also exist. Beta-carotene consists of two retinyl groups and is enzymatically converted in the small intestine by beta-carotene dioxygenase into retinol, a form of vitamin A. Carotene can be stored in the liver and converted into vitamin A as needed, making it a provitamin. Certain foods are particularly rich in carotenes, including sweet potatoes, carrots, kale, spinach, cantaloupe, turnip greens, winter squash, collard greens, cilantro, fresh thyme, romaine lettuce, goji berries, ivy gourd, cassava, and mango. The absorption of carotenes from these foods is enhanced when consumed with dietary fats, as carotenes are fat-soluble. Cooking these foods briefly can also improve absorption by breaking down plant cell walls and releasing the pigment. The two main isomers of carotene, α-carotene and β-carotene, differ in the arrangement of double bonds in their cyclic end groups. β-Carotene is the more prevalent form and is found in yellow, orange, and green leafy fruits and vegetables such as carrots, spinach, lettuce, tomatoes, sweet potatoes, broccoli, cantaloupe, oranges, and winter squash. Generally, the deeper the color of the fruit or vegetable, the higher its β-carotene content. While β-carotene is present in yellow bell peppers, it is not the primary pigment in red bell peppers or other Capsicum species. In plants, carotenoids serve various functions, including attracting pollinators and seed dispersers, as well as protecting cells from ultraviolet light damage. β-Carotene also acts as an antioxidant, neutralizing harmful free radicals in the body. However, the efficacy of β-carotene as a dietary supplement for cancer prevention remains controversial. β-Carotene is fat-soluble. Clinical trials have demonstrated that synthetic β-carotene supplements, such as those in pill form, may increase the risk of lung and prostate cancer, as well as overall mortality in smokers. These adverse effects have not been observed with naturally occurring β-carotene in foods. For instance, a 1994 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found no reduction in lung cancer incidence among participants taking β-carotene and vitamin E supplements. In fact, the study suggested potential harmful effects. Similarly, a 1996 study in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute reported an increased risk of lung cancer in individuals taking β-carotene supplements. A 2007 Cochrane Collaboration review of randomized controlled trials concluded that β-carotene supplementation increased mortality by 5%. Excessive consumption of carotene can lead to a condition called carotenemia or hypercarotenemia, characterized by yellowing of the skin (carotenodermia). Unlike vitamin A toxicity, hypercarotenemia is not harmful. It is most commonly associated with overconsumption of carrots but can also indicate underlying medical conditions. A randomized trial investigating β-carotene and vitamin A for lung cancer prevention was terminated early due to an observed increase in lung cancer incidence among smokers and individuals exposed to asbestos. The majority of synthetic carotene is produced at a manufacturing facility in Freeport, Texas, owned by DSM. In Spain, natural β-carotene is derived from the fungus Blakeslea trispora by Vitatene. In Australia, organic β-carotene is extracted from the marine algae Dunaliella salina, cultivated in harvesting ponds in Karratha, Western Australia. Carotene is also present in corn and the milk of Guernsey cows, giving the milk a yellow hue. Two primary methods are used for the total synthesis of β-carotene. The first, developed by BASF, utilizes the Wittig reaction, while the second, created by Hoffman-La Roche, employs a Grignard reaction based on earlier work by Inhoffen and colleagues. Both methods are symmetrical, with the BASF synthesis involving a C20 + C20 approach and the Hoffman-La Roche synthesis using a C19 + C2 + C19 strategy. Carotenes are a subclass of carotenoids that lack oxygen atoms, distinguishing them from xanthophylls, which contain oxygen. The β-carotene molecule has two identical β-rings at its ends, while α-carotene has one β-ring and one ε-ring. Other carotene variants include γ-carotene (β-ring and an uncyclized end, ψ), δ-carotene (ε-ring and an uncyclized end, ψ), and ε-carotene (two ε-rings). According to the systematic nomenclature: α-carotene is β,ε-carotene, β-carotene is β,β-carotene, γ-carotene is β,ψ-carotene, δ-carotene is ε,ψ-carotene, ε-carotene is ε,ε-carotene. Six micrograms of dietary β-carotene provide the equivalent of one microgram of retinol or one Retinol Equivalent (RE), which corresponds to approximately 3⅓ International Units (IU) of vitamin A.
